Interlocutor

/in-ter-LOK-yuh-ter/ - the stress falls on LOK · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Interlocutor means a person who takes part in a dialogue or conversation.

A good oral exam needs a real interlocutor: the examiner asks, listens, and follows up, so the candidate is conversing rather than reciting.

Worked Example

The chess columnist writes as though a skeptical interlocutor sat across the desk: every paragraph answers a question no one has asked aloud — 'But why not take the pawn?' — and the column reads like half of a very good conversation.

Interlocutor is the formal word for a person inside a conversation — the one you are talking WITH, not merely to. An audience receives; a bystander overhears; an interlocutor answers back, and the exchange needs that second voice to exist.

How Interlocutor Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

conversationalist

conversationalist: praises someone's skill at conversation; interlocutor just names the role of taking part

counterpart

counterpart: the person across the table in talks — your opposite number, who may say nothing

Antonyms

bystander

bystander: present at the scene but outside the exchange

eavesdropper

eavesdropper: listening in secretly, invisible to the conversation

How Strong Is It? — eavesdropper → onlooker → interlocutor

eavesdropper vs. interlocutor

eavesdropper vs. interlocutor: An eavesdropper stops far short of an interlocutor, hiding outside the exchange it secretly follows.

onlooker vs. interlocutor

onlooker vs. interlocutor: An onlooker goes a step further than an eavesdropper — at least visible at the talk's edge — but still short of an interlocutor, who speaks and is answered.

Sort It Out

Now place each word on the right side of interlocutor.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — inter

Prefix — inter: between (Latin)

Root — locut

Root — locut: spoken (Latin loqui, locutus)

Suffix — or

Suffix — or: one who

Put it together

Put it together: Inter- ('between') plus locutus ('spoken') plus -or ('one who') assembles the word exactly: one who speaks between — a person inside the back-and-forth of talk. It shares its speaking root with grandiloquence, this unit's word for puffed-up language, though an interlocutor only has to answer, not to orate.

Use the root in a new word: elocution

Use the root in a new word: elocution: Debate students run elocution drills to sharpen their delivery, repeating one line until every syllable lands.

Root Check

Word Choice

formal / academic

Interlocutor appears in philosophy, diplomacy and linguistics: the person one converses with. In everyday talk, say partner or simply 'the other person.' Counterpart fits negotiations; conversationalist praises skill. Use interlocutor when the exchange itself is under discussion and the role needs a precise name.
